procedural_history.impugned_order: Order under section 47(3) of the Act
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court allowed the petition, opining that there was no valid order under section 47(3) of the Act.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Appeals from the judgment and orders dated October 27, 1969 etc. of the Madras High Court in Writ Petitions Nos. 2709 of 1968 etc.

directions: The matter is remitted to the State Transport Appellate Tribunal to be dealt with on merits.

issue.issue_text: Whether the determination of the number of stage carriages required on a route under Section 47(3) of the Act must be done at a stage before entertaining applications for permits, or if it can be done at the same time as considering the applications.

facts: The Regional Transport Authority (RTA) had determined the number of stage carriage permits required for a route at the same time it was considering applications for those permits.
The Appellate Tribunal and the High Court disagreed with this procedure, holding that the number of permits must be determined before applications are considered.
The Supreme Court was asked to resolve this conflict regarding the correct timing for the determination under Section 47(3) of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1939.
law: Section 47(3) of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1939, allows a Regional Transport Authority to limit the number of stage carriage permits on a specified route.
Section 48 of the Act, which governs the power to grant permits, is explicitly stated to be "subject to the provisions of section 47".
Section 57 of the Act outlines the procedure for applying for permits and making representations.
application: The Court reasoned that reading Sections 47 and 57 together indicates that determining the limit on permits is a preliminary step that must occur before applications are considered.

The Court cited its own precedent in *R. Obliswami Naidu's case*, which held that fixing the limit at the same time as considering applications could harm the public interest. This is because it might give an unfair advantage to the first applicant and prevent the authority from choosing the best operator from a competitive field.
The Court emphasized that the statutory structure creates a two-step process: first, the authority must fix the limit, and only then should it entertain and consider applications for permits.

The Court pointed out that Section 48's power to grant permits is "subject to" Section 47. This means the jurisdiction to grant permits is constrained by the pre-existing limit set under Section 47(3). Therefore, the limit must be determined before the authority can grant any permits.
The Court concluded that the determination of the limit is a separate administrative decision that cannot be altered at the later stage of granting permits.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the determination of the number of stage carriages required on a route under Section 47(3) of the Act must be made at a stage before entertaining and considering applications for permits. The Court affirmed the view of the High Court and the Appellate Tribunal, establishing that fixing the limit is a distinct and prior step to the consideration of permit applications.

issue.issue_text: Whether the absence of a formal order under Section 47(3) of the Act constitutes a fatal infraction of the law.

facts: In several cases, Regional Transport Authorities (RTAs) took actions such as approving a proposal to open a new route or add a permit, conducting a traffic survey, or reaching an agreement with another region.
Following these actions, the RTAs issued public notifications under Section 57(2) of the Act, inviting applications for a specific number of permits (e.g., one permit, two permits).

Lower courts (the High Court and the State Transport Appellate Tribunal) had ruled that because there was no separate, formal order explicitly made under Section 47(3) limiting the number of permits, the process was legally invalid.
law: The Supreme Court established the principle that it is not the form but the substance of an order that matters.
Whether a valid order exists under Section 47(3) must be determined by looking at the totality of the facts and circumstances of each case.
application: The Court applied its "substance over form" test to the actions of the transport authorities.

It reasoned that when an RTA approves a proposal and then issues a notification inviting applications for a specific number of permits on a new or existing route, this sequence of events demonstrates that a decision on the limit of permits has already been made.
The notification itself, which specifies the number of available permits, serves as evidence of a prior decision that fulfills the substantive requirement of Section 47(3).
Similarly, an agreement between two states or regions to open a route and invite applications for a set number of permits also constitutes a substantive decision on the number of permits.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the absence of a separate, formal order under Section 47(3) is not a fatal infraction of the law. A valid order can be inferred from the circumstances, such as a notification inviting applications for a specific number of permits, as this shows in substance that a decision on the limit has been made.

issue.issue_text: Whether an order under Section 47(3) of the Act is invalid if made on the same day as the grant of permits, on the grounds that it does not provide sufficient time for an aggrieved person to appeal.

facts: In some appeals, the High Court and the State Transport Appellate Tribunal had found that an order under Section 47(3) (limiting the number of permits) was invalid if it was made on the same day as the order granting the permits.

The reasoning of the lower courts was that this timing did not provide a sufficient gap for an aggrieved person to appeal the order limiting the number of permits before the permits themselves were granted.
law: The Supreme Court noted that an order made under Section 47(3) is appealable.
The court also noted that the subsequent order granting the permit is also appealable.
application: The Court reasoned that the mere existence of a statutory provision allowing an appeal against an order under Section 47(3) is an "adequate answer" to the concern about the lack of time.

It further stated that the question was of "no importance" in the present case because the parties were ultimately allowed to challenge the entire proceeding, ensuring their rights were not prejudiced.
The fact that both the order limiting the permits and the order granting them are appealable provides a sufficient remedy for any aggrieved party.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument and held that an order under Section 47(3) is not invalid merely because it was made on the same day as the grant of permits. The availability of an appeal against both orders was deemed a sufficient safeguard.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the determination of the number of stage carriages required on a route under Section 47(3) of the Act must be done at a stage before entertaining applications for permits, or if it can be done at the same time as considering the applications.
appellant_arguments: The determination of the number of required stage carriages under Section 47(3) must be a preliminary step, completed before the authority considers individual applications for permits.
respondent_arguments: The authority can determine the number of stage carriages required under Section 47(3) concurrently with the consideration of the applications for permits as part of the same process.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the absence of a formal order under Section 47(3) of the Act constitutes a fatal infraction of the law.
appellant_arguments: The failure to issue a separate, formal order under Section 47(3) fixing the number of stage carriages is a fatal legal flaw that invalidates the subsequent grant of permits.
respondent_arguments: A separate, formal order is not strictly required by law, and a valid determination was made as part of the overall proceedings.

arguments.issue_text: Whether an order under Section 47(3) of the Act is invalid if made on the same day as the grant of permits, on the grounds that it does not provide sufficient time for an aggrieved person to appeal.
appellant_arguments: Making the determination under Section 47(3) on the same day as granting the permits is procedurally unfair and invalid because it denies an aggrieved party a meaningful opportunity to appeal the determination before the permits are issued.
respondent_arguments: The law does not mandate a time gap between the determination under Section 47(3) and the grant of permits; both can be lawfully done on the same day.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The validity of an order under Section 47(3) of the Act is determined by its substance, not its form. The absence of a formal order is not, in itself, a fatal infraction of the statute.
obiter: The fact that parties competed for a grant on the basis of a fixed limit and expressed no grievance at that time can be a relevant circumstance in determining the validity of an order.
An order passed under Section 47(3) of the Act is appealable.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court established that while the determination of the number of required stage carriages under Section 47(3) must, as a matter of principle, be done before applications for permits are considered, this is a requirement of substance, not form. A separate, formal order is not a fatal necessity, and a valid determination can be inferred from the circumstances, such as a notification under Section 57(2) inviting applications for a specific number of permits. Furthermore, making this determination on the same day as granting the permits is not invalid, as the statutory right to appeal the Section 47(3) order provides an adequate remedy for any aggrieved party.
legal_tests_applied: When Sections 47 and 57 of the Act are read together, the limit of the number of permits must be fixed before applications for grant of permits are invited under Section 57(2) or published under Section 57(3).
The validity of an order under Section 47(3) is a matter of substance, not form; the absence of a formal order is not a fatal infraction if a valid determination was made as part of the proceedings.
why_appellant_lost: The court rejected the argument that the absence of a separate, formal order under Section 47(3) was a fatal flaw, stating, 'We have held that it is not the (orm but the substance of the order which will have to [be considered]'.

The court dismissed the claim that a same-day determination and grant of permits was invalid because it denied an opportunity to appeal, reasoning that 'the provision for appeal agJinst an order under section 4 7(3) of the Act is an adequate answer.'

The appellants' procedural challenge was weakened by their own conduct, as 'all parties competed for the permit on the basis of the limit fixed by the R~gioilal Transport ~uthority and the decision in that behalf was conveyed to all the parties' and they 'never challenged the proceedings on the ground that there was no order under section 4 7 ( 3) of the Act' at the time.
why_respondent_won: Although the court agreed in principle that the determination of the number of permits should be a prior step, it found that in the specific facts of the case, the substance of this requirement was met through a notification under Section 57(2), which established a valid order under Section 47(3).

The court affirmed that a separate, formal order is not legally required, and that a valid determination was made as part of the overall process, stating, 'in the facts and circumstances 01 the case there was a valid order under section 4 7 ( 3) of the Act.'

The court found no legal requirement for a time gap between the determination under Section 47(3) and the grant of permits, holding that the existence of a statutory right to appeal was the sufficient legal remedy.
policy_considerations: Fixing the limit of permits before considering applications ensures that public interest remains the 'dominant consideration' and is not 'swayed by personal consideration of or predilection for the applicants.'

The determination of the number of permits must be made beforehand so that 'applicants and those who will make representations should all know the limit of number of permits to be granted in order to ensure free. a.nd fair competition.'
To maintain fairness and prevent arbitrary decisions, 'There should not be any room for elasticity of the number of permits at the time of consideration of applications for the grant.'
